claim: scNOMe-seq simultaneously measures chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and nucleosome phasing in single cells.
source: Here I adapted Nucleosome Occupancy and Methylome-sequencing (NOMe-seq) to measure chromatin accessibility and endogenous DNA methylation in single cells (scNOMe-seq).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the method measures these features, and the manuscript provides experimental data demonstrating all three measurements.

claim: scNOMe-seq recovered characteristic accessibility and DNA methylation patterns at DNase hypersensitive sites (DHSs).
source: scNOMe-seq recovered characteristic accessibility and DNA methylation patterns at DNase hypersensitive sites (DHSs).
evidence: Figure 2 shows GpC and CpG methylation patterns at DHSs in single cells matching expected patterns from bulk data.

claim: scNOMe-seq reads are sampled independently of the accessibility measurement.
source: An advantage of scNOMe-seq is that sequencing reads are sampled independently of the accessibility measurement.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the NOMe-seq method where bisulfite sequencing recovers DNA regardless of methylation status.

claim: scNOMe-seq controlled for fragment loss, enabling direct estimation of the fraction of accessible DHSs within individual cells.
source: scNOMe-seq therefore controlled for fragment loss, which enabled direct estimation of the fraction of accessible DHSs within individual cells.
evidence: Figure 2e shows quantification of accessible DHS fractions in individual cells, demonstrating this capability.

claim: scNOMe-seq provided high resolution of chromatin accessibility within individual loci.
source: In addition, scNOMe-seq provided high resolution of chromatin accessibility within individual loci which was exploited to detect footprints of CTCF binding events and to estimate the average nucleosome phasing distances in single cells.
evidence: Figures 5 and 6 demonstrate detection of CTCF footprints and nucleosome phasing at base-pair resolution.

claim: scNOMe-seq detected footprints of CTCF binding events in single cells.
source: In addition, scNOMe-seq provided high resolution of chromatin accessibility within individual loci which was exploited to detect footprints of CTCF binding events and to estimate the average nucleosome phasing distances in single cells.
evidence: Figure 5 shows CTCF footprints at individual loci in single cells, with protected motifs showing reduced GpC methylation.

claim: scNOMe-seq estimated average nucleosome phasing distances in single cells.
source: In addition, scNOMe-seq provided high resolution of chromatin accessibility within individual loci which was exploited to detect footprints of CTCF binding events and to estimate the average nucleosome phasing distances in single cells.
evidence: Figure 6 shows correlation analysis of GpC methylation at different offset distances revealing periodic patterns corresponding to nucleosome phasing.

claim: Extensive transcriptional variation between individual cells has been observed using single cell RNA-seq.
source: Extensive transcriptional variation between individual cells has been observed using single cell RNA-seq.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: Single cell RNA-seq data facilitate identification of functional subpopulations in seemingly homogeneous cell populations.
source: These data facilitate identification of functional subpopulations in seemingly homogeneous cell populations (Shalek et al., 2014), or characterization of the cellular composition of complex tissues (Jaitin et al., 2014; Treutlein et al., 2014; Macosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Single cell RNA-seq enables characterization of the cellular composition of complex tissues.
source: These data facilitate identification of functional subpopulations in seemingly homogeneous cell populations (Shalek et al., 2014), or characterization of the cellular composition of complex tissues (Jaitin et al., 2014; Treutlein et al., 2014; Macosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Measuring chromatin organization in individual cells is essential to gain mechanistic insights into regulatory features that underlie cellular heterogeneity.
source: To gain mechanistic insights into regulatory features that underlie cellular heterogeneity it is essential to measure chromatin organization in individual cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between chromatin organization and gene regulation.

claim: ATAC-seq has been adapted for single cells.
source: A number of methods that map chromatin organization in populations of cells have been adapted for single cells, including ATAC-seq (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Buenrostro et al., 2015b), DNase-seq (Jin et al., 2015), methylome sequencing (Smallwood et al., 2014; Farlik et al., 2015), and ChIP-seq (Rotem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: DNase-seq has been adapted for single cells.
source: A number of methods that map chromatin organization in populations of cells have been adapted for single cells, including ATAC-seq (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Buenrostro et al., 2015b), DNase-seq (Jin et al., 2015), methylome sequencing (Smallwood et al., 2014; Farlik et al., 2015), and ChIP-seq (Rotem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Methylome sequencing has been adapted for single cells.
source: A number of methods that map chromatin organization in populations of cells have been adapted for single cells, including ATAC-seq (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Buenrostro et al., 2015b), DNase-seq (Jin et al., 2015), methylome sequencing (Smallwood et al., 2014; Farlik et al., 2015), and ChIP-seq (Rotem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: ChIP-seq has been adapted for single cells.
source: A number of methods that map chromatin organization in populations of cells have been adapted for single cells, including ATAC-seq (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Buenrostro et al., 2015b), DNase-seq (Jin et al., 2015), methylome sequencing (Smallwood et al., 2014; Farlik et al., 2015), and ChIP-seq (Rotem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Interpretation of single cell chromatin data is complicated because of the near binary and extremely sparse signal.
source: Interpretation of these data in single cells is complicated because of the near binary and extremely sparse signal (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Buenrostro et al., 2015b; Maurano and Stamatoyannopoulos, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work describing challenges in single cell chromatin profiling.

claim: NOMe-seq employs the GpC methyltransferase (MTase) from M.CviPI to probe chromatin accessibility.
source: Nucleosome Occupancy and Methylome-sequencing (NOMe-seq) (Kelly et al., 2012) employs the GpC methyltransferase (MTase) from M.CviPI to probe chromatin accessibility (Kelly et al., 2012; Kilgore et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established methodology supported by citations.

claim: The GpC MTase methylates cytosines in GpC dinucleotides in non-nucleosomal DNA in vitro.
source: The GpC MTase methylates cytosines in GpC dinucleotides in non-nucleosomal DNA in vitro.
evidence: This is the fundamental biochemical property of the enzyme used in NOMe-seq.

claim: NOMe-seq has been used to characterize nucleosome positioning and endogenous methylation in human cell lines.
source: Combined with high-throughput bisulfite sequencing this approach has been used to characterize nucleosome positioning and endogenous methylation in human cell lines (Kelly et al., 2012; Taberlay et al., 2014) and in selected promoters of single yeast cells (Small et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: NOMe-seq has been used in selected promoters of single yeast cells.
source: Combined with high-throughput bisulfite sequencing this approach has been used to characterize nucleosome positioning and endogenous methylation in human cell lines (Kelly et al., 2012; Taberlay et al., 2014) and in selected promoters of single yeast cells (Small et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: NOMe-seq simultaneously measures chromatin accessibility through GpC methylation and endogenous CpG methylation.
source: First, NOMe-seq simultaneously measures chromatin accessibility (through GpC methylation) and endogenous CpG methylation.
evidence: This is a fundamental feature of the NOMe-seq method demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin accessibility indicates whether a putative regulatory region might be utilized in a given cell.
source: Chromatin accessibility indicates whether a putative regulatory region might be utilized in a given cell (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012), while endogenous DNA methylation in regulatory regions has been connected to a variety of regulatory processes often associated with repression (Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: Endogenous DNA methylation in regulatory regions has been connected to a variety of regulatory processes often associated with repression.
source: Chromatin accessibility indicates whether a putative regulatory region might be utilized in a given cell (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012), while endogenous DNA methylation in regulatory regions has been connected to a variety of regulatory processes often associated with repression (Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: The ability to combine complementary assays within single cells is essential for comprehensive genomic characterization of individual cells.
source: The ability to combine complementary assays within single cells is essential for a comprehensive genomic characterization of individual cells since each cell represents a unique biological sample which is almost inevitably destroyed in the process of the measurement.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the destructive nature of single cell measurements.

claim: Each sequenced read in NOMe-seq might contain several GpCs which independently report the accessibility status along the length of that read.
source: Second, each sequenced read might contain several GpCs which independently report the accessibility status along the length of that read.
evidence: This is a property of the NOMe-seq method demonstrated in the data.

claim: NOMe-seq captures additional information compared to purely count-based methods such as ATAC-seq and DNase-seq.
source: NOMe-seq therefore captures additional information compared to purely count-based methods, such as ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, which increases the confidence associated with the measurements and allows detection of footprints of individual transcription factor (TF) binding events in single cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CTCF footprint detection in Figure 5.

claim: NOMe-seq allows detection of footprints of individual transcription factor binding events in single cells.
source: NOMe-seq therefore captures additional information compared to purely count-based methods, such as ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, which increases the confidence associated with the measurements and allows detection of footprints of individual transcription factor (TF) binding events in single cells.
evidence: Figure 5 demonstrates CTCF footprint detection in single cells.

claim: In NOMe-seq, DNA is recovered and sequenced independently of its methylation status.
source: Third, the DNA is recovered and sequenced independently of its methylation status, which is a pre-requisite to distinguish between true negatives (i.e. closed chromatin) and false negatives (i.e. loss of DNA) when assessing accessibility at specified locations in single cells.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of bisulfite sequencing methods.

claim: Independent DNA recovery is a pre-requisite to distinguish between true negatives and false negatives when assessing accessibility in single cells.
source: Third, the DNA is recovered and sequenced independently of its methylation status, which is a pre-requisite to distinguish between true negatives (i.e. closed chromatin) and false negatives (i.e. loss of DNA) when assessing accessibility at specified locations in single cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for accurate single cell measurements.

claim: Allelic drop-out is pervasive in single cells.
source: This is especially important in single cells where allelic drop-out is pervasive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about single cell genomics.

claim: NOMe-seq can measure the fraction of accessible regions among a set of covered, pre-defined genomic locations in single cells.
source: In single cells, NOMe-seq can therefore measure the fraction of accessible regions among a set of covered, pre-defined genomic locations.
evidence: Figure 2e demonstrates this capability with quantification of accessible DHS fractions.

claim: NOMe-seq had previously only been performed on bulk samples before this study.
source: In this proof- of-principle study, I showed that NOMe-seq, which previously had only been performed on bulk samples (Kelly et al., 2012; Taberlay et al., 2014), can be performed on single cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents the novelty of the current work.

claim: This study profiled 19 individual GM12878 cells.
source: The scNOMe-seq datasets in this study represent 19 individual GM12878 cells and 11 individual K562 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: This study profiled 11 individual K562 cells.
source: The scNOMe-seq datasets in this study represent 19 individual GM12878 cells and 11 individual K562 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Seven GM12878 control cells were not treated with GpC MTase.
source: The set of GM12878 cells included seven control cells that were not treated with GpC MTase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Each GpC MTase-treated library was sequenced to at least 16 M individual reads.
source: Each GpC MTase-treated library was sequenced to at least 16 M individual reads (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the text and detailed in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Between 2.5M and 5M reads were retained per library after removal of duplicate reads.
source: Reads were aligned to the human genome using the aligner Bismark (Krueger et al., 2012) and, after removal of duplicate reads, between 2.5M and 5M reads were retained per library (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and detailed in Supplementary file 1.

claim: On average 6,679,864 (2.9%) of all cytosines in GpCs were covered per cell.
source: On average 6,679,864 (2.9%) of all cytosines in GpCs and 1,291,180 (3.6%) of all cytosines in CpGs were covered per cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: On average 1,291,180 (3.6%) of all cytosines in CpGs were covered per cell.
source: On average 6,679,864 (2.9%) of all cytosines in GpCs and 1,291,180 (3.6%) of all cytosines in CpGs were covered per cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DHSs were associated with strong enrichment of GpC methylation in both pooled and individual GM12878 cells.
source: DHSs were associated with strong enrichment of GpC methylation, both in data from pooled and individual GM12878 (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and K562 cells (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Figure 2a,b shows enrichment of GpC methylation at DHSs.

claim: DHSs were associated with strong enrichment of GpC methylation in K562 cells.
source: DHSs were associated with strong enrichment of GpC methylation, both in data from pooled and individual GM12878 (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and K562 cells (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4 show enrichment of GpC methylation at DHSs in K562 cells.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation decreased around the center of DHSs.
source: Conversely, endogenous CpG methylation decreased around the center of the DHSs in agreement with previous reports (Stadler et al., 2011; Ziller et al., 2015) (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 2a shows decreased CpG methylation at DHS centers, consistent with cited literature.

claim: The majority (>85%) of DHSs are detectable by NOMe-seq due to frequent occurrence of GpC di-nucleotides.
source: The frequent occurrence of GpC di-nucleotides renders the majority (>85%) of DHSs detectable by NOMe-seq (Figure 2—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplements 5 and 6 show the distribution of GpCs per DHS.

claim: 10.6% (20388/191566) of theoretically detectable DHSs had one or more GpCs covered in individual GM12878 cells.
source: Of the theoretically detectable DHSs, 10.6% (20388/191566) and 17.3% (33182/191598) had one or more GpCs covered and, using a more stringent criterion, 5.2% (9083/174896) and 9.5% (16608/174828) were covered at four or more GpCs in individual GM12878 cells and K562 cells, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: Figure 2c shows the proportion of DHSs covered in single cells.

claim: 17.3% (33182/191598) of theoretically detectable DHSs had one or more GpCs covered in individual K562 cells.
source: Of the theoretically detectable DHSs, 10.6% (20388/191566) and 17.3% (33182/191598) had one or more GpCs covered and, using a more stringent criterion, 5.2% (9083/174896) and 9.5% (16608/174828) were covered at four or more GpCs in individual GM12878 cells and K562 cells, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: Figure 2c shows the proportion of DHSs covered in single cells.

claim: 5.2% (9083/174896) of theoretically detectable DHSs were covered at four or more GpCs in individual GM12878 cells.
source: Of the theoretically detectable DHSs, 10.6% (20388/191566) and 17.3% (33182/191598) had one or more GpCs covered and, using a more stringent criterion, 5.2% (9083/174896) and 9.5% (16608/174828) were covered at four or more GpCs in individual GM12878 cells and K562 cells, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: Figure 2c shows the proportion of DHSs covered in single cells.

claim: 9.5% (16608/174828) of theoretically detectable DHSs were covered at four or more GpCs in individual K562 cells.
source: Of the theoretically detectable DHSs, 10.6% (20388/191566) and 17.3% (33182/191598) had one or more GpCs covered and, using a more stringent criterion, 5.2% (9083/174896) and 9.5% (16608/174828) were covered at four or more GpCs in individual GM12878 cells and K562 cells, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: Figure 2c shows the proportion of DHSs covered in single cells.

claim: Chromatin accessibility signal can vary along the length of a given DHS due to binding of transcription factors.
source: Chromatin accessibility signal can vary along the length of a given DHSs due to binding of transcription factors (Neph et al., 2012) and the specific position of a GpC within a DHS will thus affect its chance of being methylated.
evidence: This is supported by citation and is established knowledge about TF binding effects on accessibility.

claim: The average GpC methylation at covered DHSs in single cells was strongly correlated with the observed DNaseI accessibility at these sites in bulk populations.
source: In single cells, the average GpC methylation at covered DHSs was strongly correlated with the observed DNaseI accessibility at these sites in bulk populations (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplements 7 and 8 show correlation between GpC methylation and DNase peak scores.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation was lowest for DHSs with the highest DNaseI accessibility.
source: The opposite trend was observed for endogenous CpG methylation which was lowest for DHSs with the highest DNaseI accessibility (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 7 shows inverse relationship between CpG methylation and DNase accessibility.

claim: The correlation between GpC methylation and DNaseI accessibility was lower for scNOMe-seq data compared to bulk NOMe-seq data in the same cell line.
source: The correlation between GpC methylation and DNaseI accessibility was lower for scNOMe-seq data compared to bulk NOMe-seq data in the same cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 8 shows comparison of correlation coefficients between single cell and bulk data.

claim: Around 50% of the covered DHSs showed less than 25% GpC methylation in individual cells.
source: At the level of individual sites the distribution of GpC methylation suggested that around 50% of the covered DHS showed less than 25% GpC methylation in individual cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 9 shows cumulative distribution of GpC methylation at DHSs.

claim: 32–44% of all covered DHSs were determined to be accessible in single GM12878 cells using a 40% GpC methylation threshold.
source: At this GpC methylation threshold 32–44% and 26–37% of all covered DHSs were determined to be accessible in single GM12878 and K562 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: 26–37% of all covered DHSs were determined to be accessible in single K562 cells using a 40% GpC methylation threshold.
source: At this GpC methylation threshold 32–44% and 26–37% of all covered DHSs were determined to be accessible in single GM12878 and K562 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Even under the most lenient conditions less than 50% of DHSs were accessible in individual cells.
source: However, even under the most lenient conditions less than 50% of DHSs were accessible in individual cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 10 shows proportion of accessible sites under different parameter settings.

claim: The degree of DNaseI accessibility in bulk samples relates closely to the frequency of DHS accessibility in single cells.
source: Grouping the DHSs based on DNaseI accessibility in bulk samples, confirmed that the degree of DNaseI accessibility related closely to the frequency of DHS accessibility in single cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: Figure 2e shows that DHSs with higher DNase peak scores have higher accessibility frequency in single cells.

claim: The degree of DNaseI accessibility observed in DNase-seq of bulk samples reflects the frequency with which a region is accessible in individual cells.
source: This analysis leveraged the NOMe-seq-specific property that the DNA sequence is recovered independently of its accessibility status. It provided direct evidence for the notion that the degree of DNaseI accessibility observed in DNase-seq of bulk samples reflects the frequency with which a region is accessible in individual cells.
evidence: Figure 2e demonstrates this relationship between bulk DNase signal and single cell accessibility frequency.

claim: Chromatin accessibility between cells is less variable at regions with high DNaseI accessibility in bulk samples.
source: Consequently, chromatin accessibility between cells is less variable at regions with high DNaseI accessibility in bulk samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 11).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 11 shows Jaccard distances between cells grouped by DHS peak scores.

claim: Correlation of GpC methylation between individual cells is stronger at DHS loci compared to randomized locations.
source: Correspondingly, correlation of GpC methylation between individual cells is stronger at DHS loci compared to randomized locations (Figure 2—figure supplement 12).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 12 shows correlation coefficients for DHS vs randomized locations.

claim: Chromatin accessibility and endogenous methylation show characteristic patterns at gene promoters and within gene bodies.
source: Chromatin accessibility and endogenous methylation show characteristic patterns at gene promoters and within gene bodies (Schübeler, 2015; ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Average GpC methylation showed increased chromatin accessibility directly upstream of the TSS.
source: The average GpC methylation showed the expected increase of chromatin accessibility directly upstream of the TSS (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3a shows increased GpC methylation upstream of TSS.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation decreased towards the TSS.
source: In contrast, and as expected, the endogenous CpG methylation decreased towards the TSS (Figure 3b).
evidence: Figure 3b shows decreased CpG methylation at TSS.

claim: Endogenous methylation was specifically reduced at the narrow promoter region and gradually increased throughout the gene body.
source: Endogenous methylation was specifically reduced at the narrow promoter region and gradually increased throughout the gene body.
evidence: Figure 3c shows this pattern of CpG methylation across gene loci.

claim: Downstream of the transcription end site the average CpG methylation level fell back to the non-genic background level.
source: Downstream of the transcription end site (TES) the average level CpG methylation level fell back to the non-genic background level.
evidence: Figure 3c shows CpG methylation returning to background levels after TES.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation is typically increased within highly expressed genes.
source: Endogenous CpG methylation is typically increased within highly expressed genes (Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Gene body methylation was highest in highly expressed genes in single cell data.
source: This trend was clearly apparent in the single cell data where gene body methylation was highest in highly expressed genes (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3d shows increased gene body CpG methylation in highly expressed genes.

claim: In promoter regions chromatin accessibility (GpC methylation) increased with the transcript level of the adjacent gene.
source: Correspondingly, in promoter regions (−500 bp to +150 bp) chromatin accessibility (GpC methylation) increased with the transcript level of the adjacent gene (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 3e shows increased GpC methylation at promoters of highly expressed genes.

claim: Endogenous methylation was lowest in promoters of genes with high transcript levels.
source: In contrast to chromatin accessibility, endogenous methylation was lowest in promoters of genes with high transcript levels (Figure 3f).
evidence: Figure 3f shows decreased CpG methylation at promoters of highly expressed genes.

claim: Using a union set of DHSs from both cell types was sufficient to classify individual GM12878 and K562 cells into their respective cell types based on GpC methylation.
source: Of note, using a union set of DHSs from both cell types was sufficient to classify individual GM12878 and K562 cells into their respective cell types based on GpC methylation (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4a shows hierarchical clustering separating the two cell types based on GpC methylation.

claim: Both GM12878 and K562 cell types showed preferential enrichment of GpC methylation at their respective DHSs compared to DHSs identified in the other cell type.
source: While this assessment might have been influenced in part by the separate processing of the cell types, both cell types showed preferential enrichment of GpC methylation at their respective DHSs compared to DHSs identified in the other cell type (Figure 4b).
evidence: Figure 4b shows higher GpC methylation at cell-type-specific DHSs.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation at multiple sets of genomic features was sufficient to separate GM12878 and K562 cells into their respective cell types.
source: Similar to GpC methylation, endogenous CpG methylation at multiple sets of genomic features was sufficient to separate the cells into the respective cell types (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4c shows hierarchical clustering separating the two cell types based on CpG methylation.

claim: The average GpC methylation around CTCF ChIP-seq peaks in single cells recapitulated the accessibility previously observed in NOMe-seq bulk samples.
source: The average GpC methylation around CTCF ChIP-seq peaks (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) in single cells recapitulated the accessibility previously observed in NOMe-seq bulk samples (Kelly et al., 2012): Accessibility increased strongly towards the CTCF binding sites while the location of the CTCF motif at the center of the region showed low accessibility suggesting that CTCF binding protected from GpC MTase activity and thus creating a footprint of a CTCF binding event, both when averaged across data from all single cells (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and in individual cells (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 5a shows GpC methylation pattern around CTCF sites with footprint at motif.

claim: The location of the CTCF motif at the center of CTCF binding regions showed low accessibility suggesting that CTCF binding protected from GpC MTase activity.
source: The average GpC methylation around CTCF ChIP-seq peaks (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) in single cells recapitulated the accessibility previously observed in NOMe-seq bulk samples (Kelly et al., 2012): Accessibility increased strongly towards the CTCF binding sites while the location of the CTCF motif at the center of the region showed low accessibility suggesting that CTCF binding protected from GpC MTase activity and thus creating a footprint of a CTCF binding event, both when averaged across data from all single cells (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and in individual cells (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 5a shows reduced GpC methylation at CTCF motif location.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation was generally depleted around the center of CTCF binding sites.
source: In contrast, endogenous CpG methylation was generally depleted around the center of CTCF binding sites (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5a shows decreased CpG methylation at CTCF binding sites.

claim: Similar accessibility profiles, albeit less pronounced compared to CTCF, were observed for additional transcription factors EBF1 and PU.1.
source: Similar accessibility profiles, albeit less pronounced compared to CTCF, were observed for additional transcription factors, for example EBF1 and PU.1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows GpC methylation patterns at EBF1 and PU.1 binding sites.

claim: On average, two-thirds of CTCF motif instances within accessible regions showed no GpC methylation.
source: On average, two-thirds of CTCF motif instances within these accessible regions showed no GpC methylation, suggesting that CTCF binding prevented the GpC MTase from methylating the cytosines within the binding motif and thus creating a footprint (Figure 5d and f).
evidence: Figure 5d and f show quantification of CTCF footprints in accessible regions.

claim: Motifs associated with a footprint had significantly higher scores than motifs without a footprint.
source: Of note, motifs associated with a footprint had significantly higher scores than motifs without a footprint suggesting that the motif score is a strong determinant of CTCF binding within these accessible regions (p= 5.429e-12, paired t-test) (Figure 5e,g and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 5e,g show higher motif scores for regions with footprints, with statistical significance.

claim: CTCF footprints could be observed at individual loci within individual cells and were shared across cells.
source: Of note, the CTCF footprints could be observed at individual loci within individual cells and were shared across cells (Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 5 show CTCF footprints at specific loci across multiple cells.

claim: The pattern of GpC methylation adjacent to CTCF sites suggested that scNOMe-seq detected well-positioned nucleosomes flanking these regions.
source: The pattern of GpC methylation adjacent to CTCF sites suggested that scNOMe-seq also detected the well-positioned nucleosomes flanking these regions (Figure 5a) (Kelly et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 5a shows oscillatory GpC methylation pattern consistent with nucleosome positioning.

claim: The oscillatory distribution of average GpC and CpG methylation around locations of well-positioned nucleosomes confirmed nucleosome detection.
source: This observation was confirmed by the oscillatory distribution of the average GpC and CpG methylation around locations of well-positioned nucleosomes identified from MNase-seq data (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) (Figure 6a).
evidence: Figure 6a shows oscillatory methylation patterns at nucleosome positions.

claim: Nucleosome core particles are invariably associated with DNA fragments of 147 bp.
source: While nucleosome core particles are invariably associated with DNA fragments of 147 bp, nucleosomes are separated by linker DNA of varying lengths, resulting in different packaging densities between cell types and between genomic regions within a cell (Valouev et al., 2011; Schones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleosome structure supported by citations.

claim: Nucleosomes are separated by linker DNA of varying lengths, resulting in different packaging densities between cell types and between genomic regions within a cell.
source: While nucleosome core particles are invariably associated with DNA fragments of 147 bp, nucleosomes are separated by linker DNA of varying lengths, resulting in different packaging densities between cell types and between genomic regions within a cell (Valouev et al., 2011; Schones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Average distances between nucleosome midpoints in single cells (phasing distances) were estimated by correlating the methylation status between pairs of cytosines in GpC di-nucleotides at offset distances from 3 bp to 400 bp.
source: To determine whether scNOMe-seq data can be used to measure the average linker length, average distances between nucleosome midpoints in single cells (phasing distances) were estimated by correlating the methylation status between pairs of cytosines in GpC di-nucleotides at offset distances from 3 bp to 400 bp (Figure 6c,d and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 6c,d show correlation coefficients at different offset distances revealing periodic patterns.

claim: The estimated phases fell between 187 bp and 196 bp (mean = 196.7 bp) in GM12878 cells.
source: The estimated phases fell between 187 bp and 196 bp (mean = 196.7 bp) in GM12878 cells, and between 188 bp and 200 bp (mean = 194.2 bp) in K562 cells (Figure 6e).
evidence: Figure 6e shows distribution of estimated phase lengths.

claim: The estimated phases fell between 188 bp and 200 bp (mean = 194.2 bp) in K562 cells.
source: The estimated phases fell between 187 bp and 196 bp (mean = 196.7 bp) in GM12878 cells, and between 188 bp and 200 bp (mean = 194.2 bp) in K562 cells (Figure 6e).
evidence: Figure 6e shows distribution of estimated phase lengths.

claim: Phase estimates from scNOMe-seq are in general agreement with phase estimates derived from MNase-seq data in human cells.
source: These estimates are in general agreement with phase estimates derived from MNase-seq data in human cells (Valouev et al., 2011).
evidence: This comparison to published MNase-seq data validates the phasing estimates.

claim: Estimated phasing distances varied within individual cells depending on the chromatin context.
source: In addition, estimated phasing distances varied within individual cells depending on the chromatin context, similar to observation from bulk MNase-seq data (Valouev et al., 2011) (Figure 6f).
evidence: Figure 6f shows variation in phasing distances across different chromatin states.

claim: scNOMe-seq simultaneously measures chromatin accessibility by GpC methylation as well as endogenous CpG DNA methylation in single cells.
source: In this study, I demonstrated that scNOMe-seq simultaneously measures chromatin accessibility by GpC methylation as well as endogenous CpG and DNA methylation in single cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion demonstrated throughout the manuscript with multiple figures.

claim: scNOMe-seq data detected chromatin accessibility at DHSs and TFBS and recapitulated NOMe-seq data obtained from bulk cells.
source: scNOMe-seq detected chromatin accessibility at DHSs and TFBS and, in aggregate, these data recapitulated NOMe-seq data obtained from bulk cells (Kelly et al., 2012).
evidence: Figures 2 and 5 demonstrate detection of accessibility at DHSs and TFBS consistent with bulk data.

claim: scNOMe-seq data detected footprints of CTCF binding.
source: scNOMe-seq data also detected footprints of CTCF binding, and was used to estimate nucleosome phasing distances.
evidence: Figure 5 demonstrates CTCF footprint detection.

claim: scNOMe-seq was used to estimate nucleosome phasing distances.
source: scNOMe-seq data also detected footprints of CTCF binding, and was used to estimate nucleosome phasing distances.
evidence: Figure 6 demonstrates nucleosome phasing estimation.

claim: Similar to other single cell genomic methods, scNOMe-seq relies on annotations obtained from bulk measurements.
source: Similar to other single cell genomic methods, scNOMe-seq relies on annotations obtained from bulk measurements (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Buenrostro et al., 2015b; Smallwood et al., 2014; Farlik et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the author and supported by citations.

claim: A limitation of single cell genomic methods is their sparse coverage which leads to high allelic drop-out.
source: A limitation of single cell genomic methods is their sparse coverage which leads to high allelic drop-out.
evidence: This is a known limitation of single cell methods.

claim: For methods in which the signal is based on counting sequenced fragments, true negatives at a specific location cannot be distinguished from false negatives that are a consequence of read loss.
source: For methods in which the signal is based on counting the sequenced fragments, such as ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, this poses a challenge since true negatives at a specific location cannot be distinguished from false negatives that are a consequence of read loss.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of count-based methods.

claim: scNOMe-seq has the unique advantage that reads are recovered independently of the signal and allelic drop-out events can be distinguished from closed or inaccessible chromatin configurations.
source: Compared to these methods, scNOMe-seq has the unique advantage, that reads are recovered independently of the signal and allelic drop-out events therefore can be distinguished from closed or inaccessible chromatin configurations.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the bisulfite sequencing approach used in NOMe-seq.

claim: Using scNOMe-seq, only about 30–50% of DHSs detected in the population were found accessible in a single cell, depending on the thresholds chosen.
source: Using this approach only about 30–50% of DHSs detected in the population were found accessible in a single cell, depending on the thresholds chosen to call a site accessible.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 10.

claim: The chance of a covered DHS being open or closed is not equally distributed across all DHSs from the population.
source: As expected, the chance of a covered DHS to being open or closed is not equally distributed across all DHSs from the population.
evidence: Figure 2e shows differential accessibility frequencies for DHSs grouped by peak score.

claim: DHSs with strong DNaseI accessibility showed a higher frequency of accessibility in single cells compared to sites with low DNaseI accessibility in the population.
source: Instead, DHSs with strong DNaseI accessibility showed a higher frequency of accessibility in single cells compared to those sites with low DNaseI accessibility in the population (Figure 2e) suggesting that the peak height is indeed directly related to the frequency with which a site is accessible in individual cells.
evidence: Figure 2e demonstrates this relationship.

claim: The peak height in bulk DNase-seq is directly related to the frequency with which a site is accessible in individual cells.
source: Instead, DHSs with strong DNaseI accessibility showed a higher frequency of accessibility in single cells compared to those sites with low DNaseI accessibility in the population (Figure 2e) suggesting that the peak height is indeed directly related to the frequency with which a site is accessible in individual cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Variation between cells could in principle be due to differential GpC MTase enzyme activity.
source: In principle, variation between cells could be due to differential GpC MTase enzyme activity.
evidence: This is a potential confounding factor considered by the author.

claim: The genome-wide levels of GpC methylation reached comparable levels in all cells.
source: However, the genome-wide levels of GpC methylation reached comparable levels in all cells and the variability between cells was not equally distributed across all DHS (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows similar overall GpC methylation levels across cells.

claim: The variability between cells was not equally distributed across all DHSs.
source: However, the genome-wide levels of GpC methylation reached comparable levels in all cells and the variability between cells was not equally distributed across all DHS (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Figure 2d shows differential variability across DHS groups.

claim: Measuring similarity of chromatin accessibility between cells was sufficient to group GM12878 and K562 cells based on their cell type of origin.
source: Measuring similarity of chromatin accessibility between cells was sufficient to group GM12878 and K562 cells based on their cell type of origin (Figure 3a).
evidence: Figure 4a shows hierarchical clustering separating the two cell types.

claim: The separation of GM12878 and K562 cells is confounded with experimental batches.
source: In this particular case, the separation is confounded with experimental batches.
evidence: The author acknowledges this potential confounding factor.

claim: Higher average GpC methylation in DHSs for the respective cell type compared to the DHSs of the other cell type indicated that scNOMe-seq can differentiate the two cell types.
source: However, higher average GpC methylation in DHSs for the respective cell type compared to the DHSs of the other cell type indicated that scNOMe-seq can differentiate the two cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 14).
evidence: Figure 4b shows cell-type-specific enrichment of GpC methylation at respective DHSs.

claim: Endogenous CpG methylation at different genomic features was sufficient to distinguish between GM12878 and K562 cell types.
source: Similarly, endogenous CpG methylation at different genomic features (DHS, 10 kb windows, gene bodies) was sufficient to distinguish between the two cell types.
evidence: Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 show separation of cell types based on CpG methylation.

claim: The approach of cell type classification should be extendable to scNOMe-seq data from samples containing mixtures of cell types.
source: This approach should be extendable to scNOMe-seq data from samples containing mixtures of cell types.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications based on the demonstrated capability.

claim: scNOMe-seq measures chromatin accessibility at GpC di-nucleotides along the entire length of a sequencing read.
source: scNOMe-seq measures chromatin accessibility at GpC di-nucleotides along the entire length of a sequencing read.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the NOMe-seq method.

claim: Most features that bind DNA are smaller than the length of 100 bp (200 bp within 200–500 bp regions in the case of paired end reads).
source: Since most features that bind DNA are smaller than the length of 100 bp (200 bp within 200–500 bp regions in the case of paired end reads), the regions covered by sequence-specific transcription factors and nucleosomes can be captured within a single fragment.
evidence: This is general knowledge about DNA-binding protein sizes and sequencing read lengths.

claim: The regions covered by sequence-specific transcription factors and nucleosomes can be captured within a single fragment in scNOMe-seq.
source: Since most features that bind DNA are smaller than the length of 100 bp (200 bp within 200–500 bp regions in the case of paired end reads), the regions covered by sequence-specific transcription factors and nucleosomes can be captured within a single fragment.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between read length and binding site size.

claim: scNOMe-seq allows direct detection of TF binding provided that their sequencing motif contains at least one GpC di-nucleotide.
source: This allows one to directly detect binding of TFs provided that their sequencing motif contains at least one GpC di-nucleotide.
evidence: This is demonstrated with CTCF footprints in Figure 5.

claim: Most motifs within regions of CTCF ChIP-seq peaks were protected from GpC methylation ('footprint').
source: I demonstrated the feasibility of this approach using CTCF binding sites. Of note, most motifs within regions of CTCF ChIP-seq peaks were protected from GpC methylation ('footprint') (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5d,f show that two-thirds of CTCF motifs showed footprints.

claim: Scores for CTCF motifs that were associated with a footprint were significantly higher than for motifs without a footprint.
source: In agreement with an inferred binding event as the cause for this protection, scores for CTCF motifs that were associated with a footprint were significantly higher than for motifs without a footprint.
evidence: Figure 5e,g show this relationship with statistical significance (p= 5.429e-12).

claim: Similar measurements of TF footprints should be feasible for many TFs provided their motifs contain a GpC dinucleotide.
source: Depending on the motif specificity of a given TF and provided that their motifs contain a GpC dinucleotide, similar measurements should be feasible for many TFs and could be used to infer the activity of a range of transcription factors in single cells or to measure combinatorial binding of two or more TFs.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications based on the demonstrated CTCF footprinting.

claim: Estimation of average nucleosome phasing distances allows study of chromatin compaction.
source: Estimation of the average nucleosome phasing distances allows one to study chromatin compaction and complements the measurements of chromatin accessibility at regulatory regions and DNA methylation.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of phasing measurements.

claim: The estimates of nucleosome phasing from individual cells fit very well with measurements made from MNase-seq data in bulk samples.
source: The estimates from individual cells fit very well with measurements made from MNase-seq data in bulk samples (Valouev et al., 2011).
evidence: This comparison validates the phasing estimates from scNOMe-seq.

claim: It remains to be established whether the variation in phasing distances between individual cells is of biological or technical nature.
source: It remains to be established whether the variation in phasing distances between individual cells is of biological or technical nature (Figure 6e).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the source of observed variation.

claim: Additional optimization or alternative amplification approaches are likely to increase the yield of scNOMe-seq substantially.
source: These proof-of-principle experiments have been performed using commercial kits for bisulfite conversion and library amplification, additional optimization or alternative amplification approaches (Smallwood et al., 2014) are likely to increase the yield substantially.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements supported by citation to alternative methods.

claim: Compared to other single cell methods, scNOMe-seq does not enrich for accessible chromatin regions and thus requires significantly more sequencing coverage.
source: Compared to other single cell methods, for example ATAC-seq, scNOMe-seq does not enrich for accessible chromatin regions and thus requires significantly more sequencing coverage.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the sequencing requirements of non-enrichment methods.

claim: It should be possible to integrate the GpC MTase treatment into microfluidic workflows and combine this method with scRNA-seq.
source: Ultimately, it should be possible to integrate the GpC MTase treatment into microfluidic workflows and combine this method with scRNA-seq, similar to recently published methods that combine scRNA-seq and methylome- sequencing (Angermueller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications supported by citation to similar combined methods.

claim: This study was primarily designed to test the feasibility of NOMe-seq in single cells and only a small number of nuclei were sequenced for each cell line.
source: This study was primarily designed to test the feasibility of NOMe-seq in single cells and only a small number of nuclei where sequenced for each cell line.
evidence: This is stated by the author as a limitation of the study design.

claim: The study setup could not be used to study cell-to-cell variation in detail.
source: As a consequence, this set up could not be used to study cell-to-cell variation in detail.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the author.

claim: scNOMe-seq will be particularly useful for studies that aim to simultaneously measure chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation.
source: scNOMe-seq will be particularly useful for studies that aim to simultaneously measure chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the method based on its demonstrated capabilities.

claim: scNOMe-seq will be especially powerful for characterization of chromatin organization in single cells from heterogeneous mixtures or complex tissues.
source: This approach will be especially powerful for the characterization of chromatin organization in single cells from heterogeneous mixtures or complex tissues, for example to samples of brain tissues or primary cancer cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications based on the method's capabilities.

claim: GM12878 cells were obtained directly from Coriell.
source: GM12878 (RRID:CVCL_7526) and K562 (RRID:CVCL_0004) cells were obtained directly from Coriell and ATCC, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: K562 cells were obtained directly from ATCC.
source: GM12878 (RRID:CVCL_7526) and K562 (RRID:CVCL_0004) cells were obtained directly from Coriell and ATCC, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 DNA dye and nuclei with DNA content corresponding to the G1-phase of the cell cycle were sorted.
source: DAPI/PacBlue channel or Violet 450/500 channel were usedto excited the Hoechst 33342 DNA dye and to gate on cells with DNA content corresponding to cells in G1 phase of the cell cycle in order to maintain similar DNA content per cell and to remove potential heterogeneity attributable to cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gating on G1 phase cells was done to maintain similar DNA content per cell and to remove potential heterogeneity attributable to cell cycle.
source: DAPI/PacBlue channel or Violet 450/500 channel were usedto excited the Hoechst 33342 DNA dye and to gate on cells with DNA content corresponding to cells in G1 phase of the cell cycle in order to maintain similar DNA content per cell and to remove potential heterogeneity attributable to cell cycle.
evidence: This is the stated rationale for the G1 gating strategy.
